lessons.title: FCAW Equipment and Setup
lessons.body: FCAW needs a wire feeder, a welding gun, a power source, and a gas regulator if you're using gas-shielded wire. For self-shielded wire, you skip the gas. In most African workshops, you'll find 240V single-phase or 380V three-phase power. A 250-amp FCAW machine like a Lincoln Power MIG 256 or a Miller Millermatic 252 works well on 240V. If you only have a 200-amp machine, use 0.9mm (0.035") wire and keep your welds under 6mm thick. The wire feeder must match your wire size: 0.9mm, 1.2mm, or 1.6mm. For 1.2mm wire, you need a feeder with knurled drive rollsânot smooth V-groove rolls, which slip on flux-cored wire. Set drive roll tension so the wire doesn't crush. Too tight and the wire deforms; too loose and it slips. A good test: hold the gun 10cm from a piece of wood, pull the trigger, and the wire should push against the wood without slipping or birds-nesting. The gun liner must be the correct size for your wire. For 1.2mm wire, use a 1.2â1.4mm liner. A worn liner causes wire feed problems. The contact tip should be 0.1mm larger than the wireâso for 1.2mm wire, use a 1.3mm tip. If the tip is too small, the wire will stick; too large, and you get poor electrical contact and erratic arcs. For gas-shielded FCAW, you need a regulator and flowmeter. Set CO2 flow to 15â20 CFH (cubic feet per hour) or 7â10 L/min. Too little flow and you get porosity; too much and you get turbulence that pulls in air. Use a 75% Argon / 25% CO2 mix for flat and horizontal welds; straight CO2 for deeper penetration on thick steel. Check for leaks with soapy water. For self-shielded wire, no gas is needed, but you must use a gun with a nozzle that directs the shielding gas that comes from the flux. Keep the nozzle cleanâspatter buildup restricts flow. Polarity matters: most FCAW wires run electrode positive (DCEP). Check the wire package. If you run the wrong polarity, the arc will be unstable and the weld will be porous. Finally, always have spare contact tips, nozzles, and liners. In many African markets, these are hard to find quickly, so stock up.

lessons.title: Flux Cored Wire Types and Selection
lessons.body: Flux-cored wire comes in two main types: gas-shielded and self-shielded. Gas-shielded wire, like E70T-1, requires an external shielding gas (usually CO2 or a mix). It gives smooth welds and good penetration. Self-shielded wire, like E71T-11, has all the shielding inside the flux coreâno gas needed. That makes it perfect for outdoor work where wind would blow away shielding gas. In Africa, where many jobs are done in open-air workshops or on-site, self-shielded wire is often the practical choice. For general fabrication on mild steel, E70T-1 (gas-shielded) is common. It runs on DCEP, has a tensile strength of 70,000 psi, and works well on 6mm to 12mm plate. For thin sheet metal (1.5mm to 3mm), use E71T-GS (self-shielded, gasless) with 0.9mm wire. It runs on DCEN (electrode negative) and gives less penetration, which is good for thin metal to avoid burn-through. For rusty or dirty steel, self-shielded wire with a rutile flux (like E71T-11) handles contamination better than gas-shielded wire. But it produces more smoke and slag. For high-deposition welding on thick steel (12mm+), use E70T-5 or E70T-6 (gas-shielded, basic flux). These wires need CO2 gas and produce a thick slag that must be chipped off. They give excellent mechanical properties but are less forgiving on dirty metal. When selecting wire, check the package for the classification: E indicates electrode, 70 or 71 is tensile strength in ksi, T means tubular (flux-cored), and the number after the dash tells the polarity and usability. For example, E71T-1 is gas-shielded, DCEP, all-position. E71T-11 is self-shielded, DCEN, all-position. E70T-4 is self-shielded, DCEN, flat/horizontal only. Always match wire to your base metal thickness and position. For vertical or overhead welding, use an all-position wire like E71T-1 or E71T-11. For flat only, you can use a high-deposition wire like E70T-4. Store wire in a dry placeâmoisture in the flux causes porosity. If wire gets damp, bake it at 120Â°C for 2 hours before use. In Africa's humid climates, keep wire in a sealed container with silica gel packets.

lessons.title: Gas-Shielded vs. Self-Shielded FCAW
lessons.body: The biggest choice in FCAW is whether to use gas shielding or not. Gas-shielded FCAW uses a separate gas cylinder to protect the weld pool. Self-shielded FCAW uses the flux inside the wire to create its own shielding gas. Each has clear advantages and disadvantages that matter in African workshops. Gas-shielded FCAW gives you a cleaner weld, less smoke, and better visibility of the arc. The slag is thinner and easier to remove. It works great indoors or in still air. But you need a gas cylinder, regulator, flowmeter, and hoses. That's extra cost and equipment to maintain. In rural areas, refilling CO2 cylinders can be a 100km trip. If the wind is blowing more than 5 km/h, the gas shield blows away and you get porosity. You can build a windbreak, but that slows you down. Self-shielded FCAW needs no gas. You can weld outside in wind, rain, or on a ladder. The equipment is simpler: just the machine, wire feeder, and gun. That makes it cheaper and more portable. But self-shielded wire produces more smokeâsometimes so much you need a respirator. The slag is thicker and harder to chip. The weld appearance is rougher. Penetration can be less consistent, especially on thick steel. For most beginners in Africa, start with self-shielded wire (E71T-11, 0.9mm or 1.2mm). It's forgiving, works anywhere, and doesn't need gas. Once you master that, switch to gas-shielded for cleaner work. For gas-shielded, use 75% Argon / 25% CO2 for flat and horizontal, or straight CO2 for deep penetration. Set flow to 15â20 CFH. For self-shielded, no gas flow to set, but keep your stickout (wire extension) at 10â15mm. Too short and the flux can't shield; too long and you lose penetration. In windy conditions, self-shielded wins every time. In a shop with a steady power supply and easy gas access, gas-shielded gives better-looking welds. Choose based on your location, budget, and the job.

lessons.title: Basic FCAW Beads and Joints
lessons.body: Start with a flat bead on a piece of 6mm mild steel plate. Clean the steel with a grinder to bare metalâno rust, paint, or oil. Set your machine: for 1.2mm self-shielded wire (E71T-11), use 180â200 amps, 22â24 volts, and wire feed speed around 6â7 m/min. For gas-shielded (E70T-1), use 200â220 amps, 24â26 volts, and 7â8 m/min. Set your stickout (distance from contact tip to workpiece) at 10â15mm. Hold the gun at a 10â15Â° drag angle (tilted back, pulling the puddle). Push angle (tilted forward) works for gas-shielded but not for self-shieldedâit causes porosity. For a straight bead, pull the trigger, move steadily across the plate. Listen for a steady crackling soundâlike frying bacon. If it pops or sputters, adjust wire speed or voltage. Keep your travel speed steady. Too fast gives a thin, convex bead with poor fusion. Too slow gives a wide, flat bead that may burn through. Aim for a bead width of 6â8mm and a height of 2â3mm. For a T-joint, tack the pieces first. Weld from one end to the other, holding a 45Â° work angle and a 10â15Â° drag angle. Use a slight side-to-side motion (about 3mm) to tie both plates together. For a butt joint on 6mm plate, leave a 2mm gap. Weld one side, then grind the back and weld the other side for full penetration. For vertical-up welding, reduce amps by 10â15% and use a triangle motion: pause at the edges, move quickly across the middle. For overhead, use lower amps (160â180) and keep the puddle small. Always chip slag after each pass with a chipping hammer, then brush with a wire brush. Inspect for porosity, undercut, or lack of fusion. If you see defects, grind them out and reweld. Practice on scrap steel until your beads are consistent. In Africa, scrap steel is cheap and availableâuse it to build muscle memory.

lessons.title: Parameter Adjustment for FCAW
lessons.body: Getting the right parameters is the difference between a strong weld and a failed one. The three main settings are voltage, wire feed speed (WFS), and travel speed. Voltage controls arc length and bead width. Wire feed speed controls amperage and penetration. Travel speed controls bead size and fusion. For 1.2mm self-shielded wire (E71T-11), start with 200 amps, 23 volts, and WFS at 6.5 m/min. For gas-shielded (E70T-1), start with 220 amps, 25 volts, and WFS at 7.5 m/min. If the arc is too short (voltage too low), you'll get a stubbing sound and the wire may stick to the plate. Increase voltage by 1 volt at a time. If the arc is too long (voltage too high), you'll get a hissing sound, excessive spatter, and a flat, wide bead. Decrease voltage. Wire feed speed: if the wire burns back to the tip, increase WFS. If the wire stubs into the plate, decrease WFS. A good rule: set WFS first to get the amperage you want, then adjust voltage to fine-tune the arc. For thin metal (3mm), use 0.9mm wire, 150â170 amps, 20â22 volts, and WFS at 5â6 m/min. For thick metal (12mm), use 1.6mm wire, 250â280 amps, 26â28 volts, and WFS at 8â9 m/min. Stickout (wire extension) also matters. For self-shielded, keep it at 10â15mm. For gas-shielded, 15â20mm. Too long and you lose shielding; too short and you clog the tip. Travel speed: for a 6mm fillet weld, move at about 20â25 cm/min. If you move too fast, the weld is narrow and may lack fusion. Too slow, and you get a wide bead with possible burn-through. Use your ears and eyes: a steady crackle means good parameters. A popping or sputtering sound means adjust voltage or WFS. In Africa, power supply can be unstable. If your machine has a voltage fluctuation problem, use a stabilizer or a generator with AVR (automatic voltage regulation). Always test on scrap before welding the actual job.

lessons.title: FCAW Defects and Remedies
lessons.body: Porosity is the most common FCAW defectâsmall holes in the weld. Causes: gas flow too low or too high (for gas-shielded), wind blowing away shielding gas, dirty base metal, damp wire, or too long stickout. Remedies: set CO2 flow to 15â20 CFH, build a windbreak, grind base metal to bare metal, store wire in a dry place, and keep stickout at 10â15mm for self-shielded or 15â20mm for gas-shielded. If you see porosity, grind it out and reweld. Slag inclusion happens when slag gets trapped in the weld. Causes: insufficient cleaning between passes, wrong travel angle (pushing instead of dragging for self-shielded), or too low amperage. Remedies: chip and brush every pass, use a 10â15Â° drag angle, and increase amps by 10â15. Lack of fusion is when the weld metal doesn't fuse to the base metal. Causes: travel speed too fast, amperage too low, or wrong gun angle. Remedies: slow down, increase WFS to raise amperage, and keep a 45Â° work angle for fillet welds. Undercut is a groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe. Causes: voltage too high, travel speed too fast, or gun angle too steep. Remedies: reduce voltage by 1â2 volts, slow down, and use a flatter gun angle. Burn-through is a hole melted through thin metal. Causes: amperage too high, travel speed too slow, or no gap for expansion. Remedies: reduce WFS, increase travel speed, and use a copper backing bar if possible. Spatter is excessive molten metal droplets around the weld. Causes: voltage too high, wire stickout too short, or wrong polarity. Remedies: reduce voltage, increase stickout, and check polarity (DCEP for most gas-shielded, DCEN for self-shielded). Wire feed problems: bird-nesting (wire tangles at the feeder) means drive roll tension too loose or liner worn. Remedies: tighten tension slightly, replace liner. In Africa, where replacement parts can be scarce, keep spares. Always clean your gun nozzle and tip every 30 minutes of welding. A clean gun prevents many defects.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between gas-shielded and self-shielded FCAW?
options: A) Gas-shielded uses flux inside the wire; self-shielded uses external gas
B) Gas-shielded requires an external shielding gas; self-shielded does not
C) Self-shielded only works on aluminum
quiz.explanation: Gas-shielded FCAW uses a separate gas cylinder, while self-shielded FCAW relies on the flux core to create shielding.

quiz.q: Which wire type is best for outdoor welding in windy conditions?
options: D) Any wire with CO2 gas
quiz.explanation: Self-shielded wire like E71T-11 does not need external gas, so wind does not blow away the shielding.

quiz.q: What is the correct polarity for most self-shielded FCAW wires?
quiz.explanation: Most self-shielded wires like E71T-11 run on DCEN, while gas-shielded wires typically run on DCEP.

quiz.q: What should you check if you get porosity in a gas-shielded FCAW weld?
options: A) Gas flow rate and wind
quiz.explanation: Porosity often comes from improper gas flow or wind blowing away the shielding gas.

quiz.q: What is the recommended stickout for self-shielded FCAW?
quiz.explanation: Self-shielded FCAW requires a stickout of 10â15 mm to allow the flux to properly shield the weld.

quiz.q: Which drive roll type is needed for flux-cored wire?
quiz.explanation: Knurled drive rolls grip the flux-cored wire better and prevent slipping.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a contact tip in FCAW?
options: A) To guide the wire and transfer current
B) To shield the arc from wind
quiz.explanation: The contact tip guides the wire and conducts welding current to it.

quiz.q: What happens if the contact tip is too small for the wire?
options: A) The wire will stick and feed erratically
B) The arc will be too long
C) The weld will be too wide
D) The gas flow will increase
quiz.explanation: A too-small tip causes the wire to bind, leading to poor feed and erratic arcs.

quiz.q: For gas-shielded FCAW, what is a typical CO2 flow rate?
quiz.explanation: 15â20 CFH provides adequate shielding without turbulence.

quiz.q: Which wire classification indicates a self-shielded, all-position wire?
quiz.explanation: E71T-11 is a self-shielded, all-position flux-cored wire.

quiz.q: What does the '70' in E70T-1 indicate?
options: B) Minimum tensile strength in ksi
quiz.explanation: The '70' indicates a minimum tensile strength of 70,000 psi.

quiz.q: Why should flux-cored wire be stored in a dry place?
options: A) To prevent rust on the wire
B) To prevent moisture in the flux causing porosity
C) To keep the wire flexible
quiz.explanation: Moisture in the flux can cause porosity and hydrogen cracking in the weld.

quiz.q: What is a good travel angle for self-shielded FCAW?
quiz.explanation: A slight drag angle helps the flux shield the weld and prevents porosity.

quiz.q: What sound indicates good FCAW parameters?
options: A) Steady crackling like frying bacon
quiz.explanation: A steady crackle means the arc is stable and parameters are correct.

quiz.q: What defect is caused by travel speed too fast?
quiz.explanation: Moving too fast does not allow enough heat to fuse the weld metal to the base metal.

quiz.q: How can you fix burn-through on thin metal?
options: C) Reduce wire feed speed and increase travel speed
quiz.explanation: Lower heat input by reducing wire feed speed and moving faster.

quiz.q: What is bird-nesting in FCAW?
options: A) A type of weld joint
B) Wire tangling at the feeder
quiz.explanation: Bird-nesting is when the wire tangles at the drive rolls, often due to loose tension or a worn liner.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see slag inclusion?
options: B) Chip and brush between passes
quiz.explanation: Thorough cleaning between passes prevents slag from being trapped.

quiz.q: What is the recommended flow rate for a 75% Argon / 25% CO2 mix?
quiz.explanation: 15â20 CFH is standard for mixed gas shielding in FCAW.

quiz.q: Which polarity is typically used for gas-shielded FCAW?
quiz.explanation: Most gas-shielded wires like E70T-1 run on DCEP.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a windbreak in gas-shielded FCAW?
options: A) To keep the welder cool
B) To prevent shielding gas from blowing away
quiz.explanation: Windbreaks protect the gas shield from being dispersed by wind.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of undercut?
options: C) Wire feed speed too low
quiz.explanation: Excessive voltage creates a wide arc that melts the base metal edges, causing undercut.

quiz.q: What is the correct work angle for a T-joint fillet weld?
quiz.explanation: A 45Â° work angle splits the heat evenly between both plates.

quiz.q: What should you do if the wire burns back to the contact tip?
quiz.explanation: Burn-back means the wire is feeding too slowly; increase WFS.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for 1.2mm self-shielded wire on 6mm steel?
quiz.explanation: 180â200 A is a good starting range for 1.2mm self-shielded wire on 6mm plate.

quiz.q: Why is self-shielded FCAW often preferred in rural Africa?
options: B) It does not require a gas cylinder
quiz.explanation: No gas cylinder means lower cost and easier portability in areas with limited gas supply.

quiz.q: What is the effect of too long a stickout in self-shielded FCAW?
options: B) Loss of shielding and porosity
quiz.explanation: Excessive stickout prevents the flux from properly shielding the weld, leading to porosity.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a chipping hammer in FCAW?
options: B) To clean the contact tip
quiz.explanation: A chipping hammer is used to remove slag after each weld pass.

quiz.q: What defect can occur if the wire liner is worn?
quiz.explanation: A worn liner causes the wire to feed inconsistently, leading to erratic arcs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended travel speed for a 6mm fillet weld?
quiz.explanation: 20â25 cm/min is a typical travel speed for a 6mm fillet weld with 1.2mm wire.
